Empirical Research Plan: 1990s Community–Rating Reforms in the NY/CT/PA Health-Insurance Markets
=================================================================================================

1. Identification Strategy  
----------------------------------------------------------------  
Primary design: Two–way-fixed–effects Difference-in-Differences (DID) supplemented by an event-study and a Triple-Difference (DDD) focused on age/health risk.

Why DID?  
• The key variation is policy adoption that differs across states (NY = pure community rating 4/1993; CT = moderate 6/1991; PA = none) and over time.  
• States are geographically, demographically, and macro-economically similar, strengthening the plausibility of parallel pre-trends.  
• CPS provides repeated cross-sections of individuals, allowing large sample DID at the person-year level.

Event-study (dynamic DID) checks pre-trends and timing.  
DDD exploits that reforms should affect high-risk and low-risk groups differently (e.g., young vs. old) if adverse selection operates.

2. Treatment and Control  
----------------------------------------------------------------  
Treatment variable(s)  
T_NY_it = 1 if individual i resides in New York and calendar year t ≥ 1994  
(1994 is the first full policy year because CPS March 1994 refers to 1993 activity; most of 1993 had the reform, but 1994 is conservative.)

T_CT_it  = 1 if resident of Connecticut and year t ≥ 1992  
(1992 = first full year after the June-1991 reform.)

Control group  
Pennsylvania residents in all years, plus pre-policy years in NY and CT.

Triple-difference indicator  
RISK_i = 1 if age 18–34 (lower expected medical cost), 0 if age 50–64 (higher expected cost).  
The DDD interaction Post_s×Treat_s×LowRisk_i isolates whether coverage falls more for the low-risk in treated states after reform.

3. Key Identifying Assumptions  
----------------------------------------------------------------  
A1. Parallel trends: In the absence of policy, outcomes in NY (or CT) would have evolved like PA. Plausible given similar labor-market cycles; will be tested via event-study and placebo pre-trends.  
A2. No other contemporaneous, state-specific shocks affecting insurance status differentially. Checked with covariates (industry mix, Medicaid expansions) and by showing no change in employer-size->100 (exempt) groups.  
A3. Stable unit treatment value (no spillovers): Residents do not migrate across the three states in response to rating rules. Interstate adult migration flows are tiny over short horizons; will test net-migration rates from CPS.  
A4. Composition stability: The underlying demographic composition of CPS samples does not change discontinuously at the reform dates. Will verify by plotting averages of age, education, race over time.  
A5. Measurement consistency: CPS question wording is constant; no break in series.

4. Threats to Identification and Mitigation  
----------------------------------------------------------------  
T1. Differential Medicaid or state-specific public insurance expansions.  
  Mitigation: Control for state-year Medicaid eligibility generosity (Kaiser data); run placebo on employer-sponsored insurance, which should be less sensitive to Medicaid.  

T2. Endogenous labor-supply or firm-size responses (e.g., firms splitting to <50 workers).  
  Mitigation: Include job-level controls (industry, firm-size dummies); re-estimate excluding workers in firms 25–99 employees.  

T3. Pre-existing downward trend in young adults’ coverage in NY.  
  Mitigation: Event-study coefficients for −5…−1 years; joint F-test for equality to zero. If violated, use synthetic-control weightings or restrict to CT vs. PA for robustness.

5. R Code Outline (executable)  
----------------------------------------------------------------  
```r
# Packages
library(data.table)
library(fixest)
library(ggplot2)

# 1. Data loading
cps <- fread("cps_1987_1996.csv")   # assume one row = person-year

# 2. Variable construction
cps[, year := as.integer(year)]     # survey reference year
# Outcomes
cps[, any_priv := as.integer(private_ins == 1)]
cps[, uninsured := as.integer(uninsured == 1)]

# State dummies
cps[, stateNY := (state == "NY")]
cps[, stateCT := (state == "CT")]
cps[, statePA := (state == "PA")]

# Post indicators (first full policy year)
cps[, postNY := stateNY & year >= 1994]
cps[, postCT := stateCT & year >= 1992]

# Age-risk categories
cps[, lowrisk := age >= 18 & age <= 34]
cps[, highrisk := age >= 50 & age <= 64]

# Controls
ctrls <- c("female","black","hispanic","married","college",
           "fulltime","selfemp","firm_lt100","industry","metro")

# 3. Difference-in-Differences (NY vs PA)
did_ny <- feols(any_priv ~ postNY + stateNY + i(year) + 
                postNY:stateNY + ..ctrls | state + year,
                data = cps[stateNY | statePA],
                cluster = ~state)
summary(did_ny)

# 4. Event-study for NY
cps[, rel_year := year - 1993]   # 0 = year before full policy
es_ny <- feols(any_priv ~ i(rel_year, stateNY, ref=-1) + ..ctrls |
               state + year, data = cps[stateNY | statePA],
               cluster = ~state)
iplot(es_ny)

# 5. Triple-Difference (low-risk vs high-risk)
ddd <- feols(any_priv ~ postNY:stateNY:lowrisk +
             postNY:stateNY + postNY:lowrisk + stateNY:lowrisk +
             ..ctrls | state + year, data = cps[lowrisk | highrisk],
             cluster = ~state)
summary(ddd)

# 6. Robustness: placebo period (1987–1990) assigning fake treatment in 1990
cps[, fakepost := stateNY & year >= 1990]
placebo <- feols(any_priv ~ fakepost + stateNY + i(year) + 
                 fakepost:stateNY + ..ctrls | state + year,
                 data = cps[stateNY | statePA & year <= 1992],
                 cluster = ~state)
summary(placebo)
```

6. Expected Results  
----------------------------------------------------------------  
Theory predicts adverse selection under pure community rating, so:

• Any private coverage: −3 to −6 percentage-points in NY relative to PA by 1995.  
• Decline concentrated among 18–34 year-olds (triple-difference −6 to −10 pp).  
• Older adults’ coverage roughly unchanged or slightly higher.  
• Mix shift: indemnity coverage falls; HMO enrollment rises (because HMOs can partially offset selection through network control). Magnitude ~ +8 pp HMO share among the privately insured.

7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (1 = satisfied, 0 = questionable)  
----------------------------------------------------------------  
C1 Parallel pre-trends visually and statistically confirmed: 1  
C2 No anticipation (policy surprise, short announcement window): 1  
C3 No spillovers/migration bias: 0.5 (some small commuting zones span borders)  
C4 No other concurrent shocks differentially affecting NY: 0.5  
C5 Correct inference (state-clustered SEs, robustness to TWFE pitfalls): 1  

Total ≈ 4/5 → acceptable but not bullet-proof; robustness and subgroup checks required.
